\chapter{Comeis and Vivis}
\label{ch:spanish-er-ir-2pl}
\hlchaptermodality{44}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can recognise both vosotros forms and say that they are the second and last difference.}

Latin's -tis, collapsed two ways: -eis for one family, -is for the other.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[coméis · vivís]{coméis and vivís — the second difference, and the last}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-comeis-vivis}



\begin{quote}
Which form goes with \emph{vosotros} for \emph{hablar}? (\emph{Habláis}.) And where is that word used? (\emph{Spain}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two families, two endings, one lesson}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{coméis} — \emph{you all eat.}  ·  \textbf{vivís} — \emph{you all live.}
\end{quote}

These two are taught together, and it is worth saying why, because this book has otherwise insisted on one form per lesson.

You already know the fact they demonstrate. The \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} families differ in exactly \textbf{two} slots — \emph{nosotros}, which you met last chapter, and \emph{vosotros}, which is this one. Learning them apart would teach the same single fact twice and hide the pattern that makes it easy.

\textbf{And after this, the two families agree again.} \emph{They eat} and \emph{they live} take the same ending, as every singular form did.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Both descend from Latin's \textbf{-tis}: \emph{comeditis}, \emph{vīvitis}. Spanish lost the \textbf{-t-} between vowels — as it lost most of them — and what was left collapsed differently in each family. The \emph{-er} line kept two vowels, \textbf{-éis}. The \emph{-ir} line kept one, \textbf{-ís}.

Same ending, same erosion, two outcomes. That is most of what sound change looks like.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU HEAR: \textquotedblleft{}coméis\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}vivís\textquotedblright{}{]} $\to$ a Spaniard, addressing friends.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}comemos, coméis\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}vivimos, vivís\textquotedblright{} — the two differing slots, side by side
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give both \emph{vosotros} forms. (\textbf{Coméis}, \textbf{vivís}.) In how many slots do the two families differ? (\textbf{Two} — and you have now met both.) What Latin ending is behind them? (\textbf{-tis}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
